# Survey summary

<!-- Generated by survey/survey_summary.py. Do not edit by hand. -->

**Responses: 21**

> **A small, non-representative sample, and I want to say exactly how.** These 21 households came from my own student network and are mostly better-off homes; 12 of the 21 are in Islamabad or Rawalpindi. They are not a random or weighted sample of Pakistani households, so every figure below describes only the people who answered. **Next I want to survey beyond my own network, including renters and families with no solar at all**, because those are the homes this is least likely to fit today. These answers are used to choose plausible settings for the simulation, not to make claims about the country.

## What happens if the simulation matches the survey's typical solar home

I ran one extra scenario set up the way the survey's solar homes actually look: **battery on, net
metering, water motor and washing machine already at midday, and a two-hour daily power cut.**

| | Usual | Agent | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grid units bought | 50.7 | **65.4** | **+14.7** |
| Evening units (18:00-22:00) | 0 | 0 | no change |
| Solar exported | 411.9 kWh | 424 kWh | +12.1 |
| Solar wasted | 0 kWh | 0 kWh | no change |
| Estimated bill before taxes | Rs 1,000 | Rs 1,000 | no change |
| Hours with no power | 0 | 0 | no change |

**The agent makes this home slightly worse, and that is worth saying plainly.** It buys
**14.7 more units** and saves nothing at all on the bill.

The reason is that this home has already done everything the agent would suggest:

- It **already runs the motor and washing machine at midday**, so there is nothing left to shift.
- It **already has a battery**, so the evening is covered either way - evening grid units are
  0 in *both* modes.
- It is **already net-metered**, so surplus solar is credited rather than wasted. Solar wasted is
  0 kWh in both modes, and the bill is the fixed charge alone in both.

The extra units come from the agent holding battery charge back for an evening that never needed
defending, so it buys a little more during the day instead.

**This is the honest boundary of the idea.** The Solar Home Agent is for the home that is
**unregistered, has no battery, and runs its appliances in the evening** - which is the national
typical case and the default scenario in this repository. For a home that is registered,
battery-equipped and already shifting load by day, it has nothing to add. That is why this scenario
is reported here and **is not used in the video or as the headline**.

Reproduce: see `results/survey_scenario.json`.

## Suggested scenario settings

Based on the **10 respondents who reported having solar** (of 21 in total).

| Setting | Suggested | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| `has_battery` | `true` | most common answer: Yes (10 answered) |
| `export_mode` | `net_billing` | most common answer: Yes (10 answered) |
| `household` | see note below | most common units band: 100-200 units |
| `power_cuts` | see note below | most common: 2-4 hours |
| `usual_times` | see note below | most common time: Midday (11 am - 3 pm) |

Notes for translating these into the config:

- `household` is `low_use` for bands up to 200 units and `high_use` above that. If the most common band is 201-300, consider setting `calibration.low_use_target_units` from a real bill instead of switching profile.
- `power_cuts` takes hour windows, for example `[[20, 21]]` for one evening hour. Convert the reported duration into the hours your area actually loses.
- `usual_times` takes a start hour per appliance, for example `water_motor: 19`.

After editing `config/scenario.yaml`, rerun everything with:

```bash
python -m src.simulate --all --calibrate
```
